name: Command Line Mastery (macOS)
description: Become fluent with the macOS command line: mental models, core Unix concepts, powerful commands, automation patterns, and modern tools.

cards.back: A program that provides a text interface to interact with the operating system.
A program that interprets commands and runs other programs.

cards.front: What is the difference between a terminal and a shell?
cards.back: The terminal displays input/output; the shell interprets and executes commands.

cards.front: Why is text considered the universal interface?
cards.back: Because text is easy to generate, transform, log, and automate.

cards.front: What are stdin, stdout, and stderr?
cards.back: Standard input, output, and error streams used by programs.

cards.front: What does it mean that Unix tools are composable?
cards.back: Small tools can be chained together to perform complex tasks.

cards.front: What does the pwd command do?
cards.back: Prints the current working directory.

cards.front: What is the purpose of ls?
cards.back: Lists files and directories.

cards.front: What is a hidden file on macOS?
cards.back: A file whose name starts with a dot.

cards.front: What is the difference between foreground and background jobs?
cards.back: Foreground jobs block the shell; background jobs do not.

cards.front: What is the purpose of head and tail?

cards.back: It allows paging without loading the whole file.

cards.back: Reusing and auditing past commands.

cards.front: What is a safe CLI habit?
cards.back: Preview commands before executing destructive actions.

cards.front: What is the CLI’s biggest advantage over GUIs?

sampleIdeas.name: The CLI Mental Model
sampleIdeas.textDescription:
The command line is not a list of commands to memorize but a language for interacting with systems. Commands are programs, and text is the medium through which they communicate.

Understanding stdin, stdout, and pipes unlocks most of the CLI’s power.

Once this mental model clicks, new tools become easier to learn.

This mindset scales from local machines to servers.

sampleIdeas.name: Files, Paths, and Permissions
sampleIdeas.textDescription:
Everything in Unix-like systems is a file. Paths describe location, and permissions describe who can do what.

Mastering these concepts prevents common mistakes and confusion.

Symbolic links add flexibility without duplication.

These basics power nearly every task.

sampleIdeas.name: Processes and System Control
sampleIdeas.textDescription:
Processes represent running programs consuming resources.

Understanding how to inspect and signal them gives you control over your system.

Tools like top and ps provide visibility.

This is essential for debugging and performance tuning.

sampleIdeas.name: Pipes: The Unix Superpower
sampleIdeas.textDescription:
Pipes allow small tools to be combined into powerful workflows.

Instead of writing new programs, you connect existing ones.

This is why the CLI scales so well.

Thinking in pipes changes how you approach problems.

sampleIdeas.name: Automation and Ergonomics
sampleIdeas.textDescription:
Automation turns repeated effort into reusable scripts.

Aliases, functions, and dotfiles shape your environment.

Modern tools like fzf and ripgrep improve speed dramatically.

Good ergonomics compound over time.

sampleIdeas.name: Safe Destructive Commands
sampleIdeas.textDescription:
Commands like rm, mv, and sed can destroy data instantly.

Always preview output.

Use -i flags when available.

Backups matter.

sampleIdeas.name: CLI Debugging Patterns
sampleIdeas.textDescription:
Debugging from the CLI is faster when you inspect state.

Use echo, set -x, and small test commands.

Reduce scope.

Observe outputs.
